facts.claim: Anthropic: structured outputs guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding, apart from the cases its docs list (a refusal, or hitting max_tokens); your JSON schema is compiled into a set of rules (a grammar) that limits what Claude can write.

Anthropic: objects must set additionalProperties to false; recursive schemas, number limits (minimum, maximum, multipleOf) and string length limits (minLength, maxLength) are not supported, and an unsupported feature returns a 400 error.
Anthropic: the first time you use a schema there is extra latency while the grammar compiles; compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use.

Anthropic: when Claude refuses, the response has stop_reason "refusal", you are billed for the tokens generated, and the output may not match your schema, because the refusal takes precedence over the schema.
Anthropic: when the answer hits max_tokens, the output may be incomplete and not match your schema; retry with a higher max_tokens.
Anthropic’s docs (checked 2026-10-30): the context window holds the prompt and the answer Claude writes; current Claude models have a 1M-token window, and one request can write up to 128k tokens.
OpenAI (August 2024, vendor-reported): on its own test of following complex JSON schemas, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with Structured Outputs scored 100%, while the older gpt-4-0613 scored less than 40%.
OpenAI: JSON mode gives valid JSON, but only Structured Outputs ensure the answer follows your schema.
OpenAI: every field must be required and additionalProperties must be false; a schema may have up to 5,000 object properties, 10 levels of nesting and 1,000 enum values.
OpenAI: a refusal comes back in its own refusal field and may not follow your schema, so check for it before parsing.
OpenAI: an answer can be cut off when it reaches the max tokens limit; the response is then marked incomplete and should not be parsed as finished.

XGrammar (Dong and colleagues, 2024) is an engine that limits a model to text a set of rules (a grammar) allows; it splits the vocabulary into tokens that can be checked ahead of time and tokens checked while writing, and its authors report up to 100× speedup over earlier engines.

llguidance works out the mask in about 50 microseconds (millionths of a second) of one processor core per token, for a 128k-token vocabulary; its README says it powers OpenAI’s Structured Outputs (JSON Schema) and is built into vLLM and llama.cpp.

Guidance's token healing backs up one or more tokens before the end of the prompt and makes the first generated tokens start with that text, so the model can use the split it learned in training. A trailing space in a prompt is almost always a bad idea in GPT models.
